# Camera Network Sensitivity Calibration: lessons from the field (summary)

Isolde Brindale, lead engineer on the wildfire detection camera network project, presented on improving camera sensitivity calibration to reduce false alarms caused by dust and fog. The network covers 1,200 cameras across high-risk zones, monitoring vegetation and wildfire indicators. Over 18 months, her team executed a three-phase project involving data collection during dust and fog seasons, development of a dynamic threshold algorithm responsive to environmental conditions, and field deployment on 300 cameras with significant false alarm reduction. Key insights include the integration of weather station data for more precise adjustments and the necessity of seasonal recalibration to maintain accuracy. Plans to scale the adaptive calibration across the full network and incorporate machine learning for enhanced threshold tuning were also discussed.

- The project involved 1,200 cameras across Northern Ridge and Southern Valley zones to monitor wildfire risks.
- A dynamic thresholding algorithm was developed to adjust sensitivity by up to 15% during dust storms and fog events.
- Field tests on 300 cameras resulted in a 42% reduction in false alarms and a 30% decrease in unnecessary utility dispatches.
- Integration of weather station data and monthly automated recalibration improved detection precision and long-term reliability.
- Future plans include deploying machine learning models to refine threshold adjustments beyond current rule-based methods.
